newsitem.title: CHINA: Long-awaited GM, China deal clinched by Gore.
newsitem.headline: Long-awaited GM, China deal clinched by Gore.

text.p: General Motors Corp and China's state-owned Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp on Tuesday signed a long-awaited $1.57 billion joint venture to produce medium-sized sedans in Shanghai.

The agreement that gives the U.S. car giant a foothold in the domestic luxury car market was signed in a ceremony in the Great Hall of the People by General Motors chairman John Smith and Chen Xianglin, president of Shanghai Automotive.
It was witnessed by visiting U.S. Vice President Al Gore.

General Motors and Shanghai Automotive will each hold a 50 percent stake in the $1.57 billion venture, which includes a sedan manufacturing plant and a design and engineering centre, Smith told a news conference after the signing.
Gore's fence-mending visit to China had helped to put the final stamp of approval on the deal, which had been in the works since 1994, Smith said.
"We were in pretty good shape on the agreement and the circumstances of Vice-President Gore's visit obviously provided the catalyst to bring it together," Smith said.
Although Gore's trip may have helped to win Beijing's blessing, the venture failed to gain a much sought-after exemption from a duty on imports of capital goods.
"We are very specific on the fact that there is no waiver," Rudolph Schlais, president of General Motors China Operations, said.

Industry analysts had speculated that Beijing would grant the huge project a special waiver from a change in China's tax law that removed exemptions for foreign invested companies on imports of capital goods.
GM officials declined to say how much the import duty would cost the Shanghai-based plant but said the failure to secure a waiver would affect initial profits.
"Obviously, the changes in tax do affect the returns on the project," Smith said. "However this is still a good programme."
The new firm, Shanghai GM, would import nearly $1.6 billion worth of goods from the United States, Smith said but did not say what portion of that would be subject to the tax.
The plant would have a production capacity of 100,000 Buick sedans a year, Smith said, adding that the factory would start up in late 1998 and would produce 50,000 cars a year by 2000.
The Buicks, powered by a 2.98-litre V6 engine, would compete with domestically produced Audis and Red Flags and imports of luxury cars such as Japan's Lexus, officials said.
Officials dismissed speculation that the firm would suffer in fiercer competition from imports if China won entry to the World Trade Organisation.
"Using the homefield advantage here in China, we intend to compete aggressively against luxury imports," Smith said.
The venture would initially target institutional buyers but an increasing portion of China's 1.2 billion people would become private car buyers over the next decade, Smith said.
"The product will be competitively priced. We are going into the market to be competitively priced, with a quality product," Schlais said.
The venture must still win final approval from the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation before it can start operation, said Shanghai Automotive's Chen.
